title: Hydrogen
description: Master Class 11 Chemistry Hydrogen: dual position, isotopes, preparation, hydrides, water, hardness removal, heavy water, H2O2 and hydrogen as fuel with solved examples and tests on Vidaara.

topics.title: Hydrogen: Position, Isotopes & Preparation
topics.concept:
Hydrogen (Z = 1, configuration 1s1) is the lightest and most abundant element in the universe. Although it has just one electron, it refuses to sit comfortably in any single group of the periodic table.

Dual position in the periodic table

Like the alkali metals (Group 1) it has one valence electron (ns1), forms a unipositive ion H+, and acts as a reducing agent. Like the halogens (Group 17) it is one electron short of a noble-gas configuration, exists as a diatomic molecule H2, has high ionisation enthalpy and can gain an electron to form the hydride ion H−. Because it fits neither group perfectly, hydrogen is given a unique position at the top of the table.

Isotopes of hydrogen

Hydrogen has three isotopes, all with one proton but differing in neutrons:

  • Protium (11H): no neutron, ≈ 99.985%, ordinary hydrogen.
  • Deuterium (21H or D): one neutron, ≈ 0.015%, found in heavy water D2O.
  • Tritium (31H or T): two neutrons, radioactive (β-emitter, half-life ≈ 12.3 years), present in traces.

Since they have identical electronic configurations, the isotopes show the same chemical behaviour but differ in rate of reaction (deuterium reacts more slowly — the kinetic isotope effect) and in physical properties such as density and boiling point.

Occurrence

In the free state hydrogen is rare on Earth (the atmosphere holds only traces) because it is too light to be held by gravity. In the combined state it is everywhere — chiefly as water (H2O), and in all acids, bases, hydrocarbons and living matter.

Methods of preparation

Laboratory: by the action of dilute sulphuric acid on granulated zinc — Zn + H2SO4 → ZnSO4 + H2. Very pure hydrogen comes from the electrolysis of acidified or barium-hydroxide water.

Commercial: (i) Electrolysis of warm acidified water between platinum electrodes gives H2 at the cathode. (ii) Water gas / syngas: passing steam over red-hot coke at about 1270 K gives a mixture of CO and H2 called water gas — C + H2O → CO + H2. In the water-gas shift reaction the CO is removed by reacting it with more steam over an iron-chromate catalyst: CO + H2O → CO2 + H2; the CO2 is scrubbed out under pressure to leave pure dihydrogen.

Properties

Physical: colourless, odourless, highly combustible gas; the lightest known substance; sparingly soluble in water. Chemical: the H–H bond is strong (435.9 kJ mol−1), so hydrogen is fairly unreactive cold but reactive when heated — it burns in oxygen to water, combines with halogens, reduces hot metal oxides, and hydrogenates unsaturated oils over nickel.

examples.problem: Give two properties of hydrogen that resemble the alkali metals and two that resemble the halogens.
examples.solution:
1. Like alkali metals: it has a single valence electron (ns1) and forms a unipositive ion H+; it also acts as a reducing agent.
  2. Like halogens: it is one electron short of a noble-gas configuration and exists as a diatomic molecule H2; it can gain an electron to form the hydride ion H− and has a high ionisation enthalpy.
  3. Because it shares features of both, it is given a unique position in the periodic table.

Answer: Alkali-like: one valence electron / forms H+. Halogen-like: diatomic molecule / forms H−.

examples.problem: Name the three isotopes of hydrogen and state the number of neutrons in each.
examples.solution:
1. Protium (11H): mass number 1, so neutrons = 1 − 1 = 0.
  2. Deuterium (21H): mass number 2, so neutrons = 2 − 1 = 1.
  3. Tritium (31H): mass number 3, so neutrons = 3 − 1 = 2.

Answer: Protium 0 neutrons, deuterium 1 neutron, tritium 2 neutrons.

examples.problem: Write the reactions involved in the manufacture of dihydrogen from water gas, including the shift reaction.
examples.solution:
1. Pass steam over red-hot coke at about 1270 K to form water gas: C + H2O → CO + H2.
  2. Carry out the water-gas shift reaction over an iron-chromate catalyst: CO + H2O → CO2 + H2.
  3. Remove CO2 by scrubbing under pressure to obtain pure dihydrogen.

Answer: C + H2O → CO + H2; then CO + H2O → CO2 + H2.

examples.problem: Why is deuterium chemically similar to but kinetically slower than protium?
examples.solution:
1. Both isotopes have the same electronic configuration (1s1), so they show the same chemical reactions.
  2. Deuterium has double the mass of protium, so the D–X bond is stronger and harder to break.
  3. This raises the activation energy and lowers the reaction rate — the kinetic isotope effect.

Answer: Identical electron configurations give identical chemistry, but the heavier D atom forms stronger bonds, so reactions of deuterium are slower.

examples.problem: Write the balanced equation for the laboratory preparation of dihydrogen and name the gas-collection method used.
examples.solution:
1. React granulated zinc with dilute sulphuric acid: Zn + H2SO4 → ZnSO4 + H2.
  2. The gas evolved is dihydrogen.
  3. Because hydrogen is insoluble in water and lighter than air, it is collected by downward displacement of water.

Answer: Zn + H2SO4 → ZnSO4 + H2; collected over water (downward displacement of water).

examples.problem: The H–H bond enthalpy is 435.9 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>. Explain how this accounts for the low reactivity of dihydrogen at room temperature.
examples.solution:
1. A high bond enthalpy means a large amount of energy is needed to break the H–H bond into atoms.
  2. At room temperature few molecules have this much energy, so reactions are very slow.
  3. On heating or with a catalyst the bond can be broken, so hydrogen becomes reactive at high temperatures.

Answer: The strong H–H bond (high dissociation enthalpy) makes hydrogen unreactive at room temperature, requiring heat or a catalyst to react.

recap: Hydrogen (1s<sup>1</sup>) has a dual position: it resembles alkali metals (one valence electron, forms H<sup>+</sup>) and halogens (diatomic, forms H<sup>−</sup>), so it is placed uniquely.
Three isotopes: protium (0 neutrons), deuterium D (1 neutron, in heavy water) and tritium T (2 neutrons, radioactive).
Lab preparation: Zn + dilute H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → ZnSO<sub>4</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>; pure hydrogen by electrolysis of acidified water.
Commercial: electrolysis of water and the water-gas route C + H<sub>2</sub>O → CO + H<sub>2</sub>, followed by the shift reaction CO + H<sub>2</sub>O → CO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>.
Dihydrogen is colourless and odourless with a strong H–H bond (435.9 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>), so it is unreactive cold but reduces metal oxides and hydrogenates oils when heated.

quiz.q: Hydrogen is placed uniquely in the periodic table because it resembles:
quiz.explanation: Hydrogen shares features with Group 1 (one valence electron, H<sup>+</sup>) and Group 17 (diatomic, H<sup>−</sup>), so it fits neither perfectly.

quiz.q: Which isotope of hydrogen is radioactive?
quiz.explanation: Tritium (<sup>3</sup>H) has two neutrons and is a beta-emitter with a half-life of about 12.3 years.

quiz.q: Water gas is a mixture of:
quiz.explanation: Steam over red-hot coke gives water gas, a mixture of carbon monoxide and dihydrogen: C + H<sub>2</sub>O → CO + H<sub>2</sub>.

quiz.q: In the laboratory, dihydrogen is usually prepared by reacting zinc with:
quiz.explanation: Zn + dilute H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → ZnSO<sub>4</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>; concentrated or oxidising acids do not give hydrogen cleanly.

topics.title: Hydrides & Water
topics.concept:
When hydrogen combines with another element it forms a hydride. The character of the hydride depends on the partner element, and the most important hydride of all — water — shapes life and chemistry on Earth.

Types of hydrides

  • Ionic (saline) hydrides: formed by the most electropositive s-block metals (e.g. NaH, CaH2). They are crystalline, non-volatile solids containing the H− ion. On electrolysis of the molten hydride, hydrogen is liberated at the anode, proving the negative charge on hydrogen. They react violently with water: NaH + H2O → NaOH + H2.
  • Covalent (molecular) hydrides: formed by p-block non-metals (e.g. CH4, NH3, H2O, HF). They are volatile, with discrete molecules held by weak van der Waals forces; those with N, O or F show hydrogen bonding, giving abnormally high boiling points.
  • Metallic (interstitial) hydrides: formed by many d- and f-block metals, with hydrogen in the interstitial holes of the lattice (e.g. Pd, Ti). They are often non-stoichiometric (e.g. TiH1.7) and store hydrogen. The d-block metals of groups 7–9 generally do not form hydrides — the hydride gap.

Structure and properties of water

Water is a bent molecule with an H–O–H angle of about 104.5°; oxygen is sp3 hybridised with two lone pairs. Strong hydrogen bonding gives water its anomalies: high boiling point, high specific heat, high surface tension, and the fact that ice (an open H-bonded cage) is less dense than liquid water, so it floats. Water is an excellent solvent and is amphoteric.

Hard and soft water

Soft water lathers readily with soap. Hard water does not, because dissolved Ca2+ and Mg2+ salts react with soap to give an insoluble scum.

  • Temporary hardness is due to the bicarbonates Ca(HCO3)2 and Mg(HCO3)2. It is removed simply by boiling (which decomposes the bicarbonate to insoluble carbonate) or by Clark's method (adding a calculated amount of slaked lime): Ca(HCO3)2 + Ca(OH)2 → 2CaCO3 + 2H2O.
  • Permanent hardness is due to the chlorides and sulphates of calcium and magnesium and is not removed by boiling. It is removed by washing soda (Na2CO3), by the permutit / zeolite process (Na2Z exchanges Na+ for Ca2+/Mg2+), or by modern synthetic ion-exchange resins that swap H+ and OH− for the dissolved ions, giving demineralised water.

Heavy water (D2O)

Heavy water is water in which both hydrogen atoms are deuterium. It is obtained by the prolonged electrolysis of ordinary water (the lighter H2O is electrolysed faster, enriching the residue in D2O) or by fractional distillation. It has a higher boiling point (101.4°C), higher density (1.106 g cm−3) and reacts more slowly than ordinary water. Its main use is as a moderator in nuclear reactors, where it slows fast neutrons without absorbing them.

examples.problem: Classify the following hydrides and give the type: NaH, CH<sub>4</sub>, TiH<sub>1.7</sub>.
examples.solution:
1. NaH is formed by an electropositive s-block metal and contains H−, so it is an ionic (saline) hydride.
  2. CH4 is formed by a p-block non-metal as discrete molecules, so it is a covalent (molecular) hydride.
  3. TiH1.7 is a non-stoichiometric d-block hydride with hydrogen in the lattice holes, so it is a metallic (interstitial) hydride.

Answer: NaH ionic, CH4 covalent, TiH1.7 metallic.

examples.problem: Why does hard water fail to give lather with soap?
examples.solution:
1. Hard water contains dissolved Ca2+ and Mg2+ ions.
  2. These ions react with the sodium stearate of soap to form insoluble calcium and magnesium stearates.
  3. The insoluble scum forms instead of lather, wasting soap.

Answer: Ca2+ and Mg2+ ions precipitate soap as an insoluble scum, so no lather forms.

examples.problem: Write the reaction by which Clark's method removes temporary hardness.
examples.solution:
1. Temporary hardness is due to the bicarbonate Ca(HCO3)2.
  2. A calculated amount of slaked lime, Ca(OH)2, is added.
  3. The reaction precipitates insoluble calcium carbonate: Ca(HCO3)2 + Ca(OH)2 → 2CaCO3 + 2H2O.

Answer: Ca(HCO3)2 + Ca(OH)2 → 2CaCO3↓ + 2H2O.

examples.problem: Explain how the zeolite (permutit) process removes permanent hardness, and how the exhausted zeolite is regenerated.
examples.solution:
1. Hard water is passed through sodium zeolite (Na2Z), which exchanges its Na+ for the Ca2+/Mg2+ in water: Na2Z + Ca2+ → CaZ + 2Na+.
  2. The water leaving the bed is soft because its hardness-causing ions are now held in the resin.
  3. When exhausted, the zeolite (now CaZ) is regenerated by flushing it with a concentrated brine (NaCl) solution: CaZ + 2NaCl → Na2Z + CaCl2.

Answer: Na2Z swaps Na+ for Ca2+/Mg2+ to soften water; regenerated with brine: CaZ + 2NaCl → Na2Z + CaCl2.

examples.problem: Ice floats on water. Explain this anomaly using the structure of water.
examples.solution:
1. In liquid water, hydrogen bonds form and break, allowing molecules to pack fairly closely.
  2. In ice, each water molecule is hydrogen-bonded to four others in an open, cage-like tetrahedral network.
  3. This open structure has more empty space, so ice is less dense than liquid water and therefore floats.

Answer: The open hydrogen-bonded cage of ice has a lower density than liquid water, so ice floats.

examples.problem: How is heavy water obtained and why is it used in nuclear reactors?
examples.solution:
1. Heavy water D2O is obtained by the prolonged electrolysis of ordinary water; the lighter H2O is electrolysed faster, so the residue is enriched in D2O.
  2. It can also be concentrated by fractional distillation.
  3. In a reactor it acts as a moderator: it slows down fast neutrons by collisions without absorbing them, helping sustain the chain reaction.

Answer: Made by prolonged electrolysis of water; used as a neutron moderator in nuclear reactors.

recap: Hydrides are ionic/saline (NaH, CaH<sub>2</sub>; contain H<sup>−</sup>), covalent/molecular (CH<sub>4</sub>, NH<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>O) or metallic/interstitial (Pd, Ti hydrides; store hydrogen).
Water is a bent molecule (H–O–H ≈ 104.5°) whose hydrogen bonding gives high boiling point, high specific heat and floating ice.
Temporary hardness (bicarbonates) is removed by boiling or Clark's method: Ca(HCO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> + Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> → 2CaCO<sub>3</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O.
Permanent hardness (chlorides/sulphates) is removed by washing soda, the zeolite/permutit process, or synthetic ion-exchange resins.
Heavy water D<sub>2</sub>O, made by prolonged electrolysis, is denser and slower-reacting and is used as a moderator in nuclear reactors.

quiz.q: Which of these is an ionic (saline) hydride?
quiz.explanation: NaH is formed by an electropositive s-block metal and contains the H<sup>−</sup> ion, making it an ionic hydride.

quiz.q: Temporary hardness of water is caused by:
quiz.explanation: Temporary hardness is due to Ca(HCO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> and Mg(HCO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>, removed by boiling or Clark's method.

quiz.q: Permanent hardness of water can be removed by:
quiz.explanation: Permanent hardness (chlorides/sulphates) is not removed by boiling; the zeolite or ion-exchange process swaps the Ca<sup>2+</sup>/Mg<sup>2+</sup> ions out.

quiz.q: Heavy water is mainly used as a:
quiz.explanation: D<sub>2</sub>O slows fast neutrons without absorbing them, so it acts as a moderator in nuclear reactors.

topics.title: Hydrogen Peroxide & Hydrogen as Fuel
topics.concept:
Hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) is one of the most useful oxygen compounds of hydrogen, and dihydrogen itself is increasingly viewed as the clean fuel of the future.

Preparation

In the laboratory, dilute sulphuric acid is added to barium peroxide: BaO2·8H2O + H2SO4 → BaSO4 + H2O2 + 8H2O; the insoluble BaSO4 is filtered off. Industrially it is made by the auto-oxidation of 2-ethylanthraquinol (the anthraquinone process).

Structure (open-book)

The H2O2 molecule is non-planar with an open-book structure: the two O–H bonds lie in two different planes that meet along the O–O bond, like a half-open book. In the gas phase the dihedral angle is about 111° (about 90° in the solid), the O–O bond about 148 pm and each O–H bond about 95 pm. Pure H2O2 is a colourless, syrupy liquid, denser than water and miscible with it; it is sold as a 30% solution or a dilute 3% antiseptic.

Chemical properties — both oxidising and reducing

The oxygen in H2O2 is in the −1 state, midway between 0 and −2, so it can either gain or lose electrons, acting as both oxidising and reducing agent.

  • Oxidising (acidic): 2Fe2+ + H2O2 + 2H+ → 2Fe3+ + 2H2O; it also turns black PbS to white PbSO4, restoring old paintings.
  • Reducing (acidic): it decolourises acidified KMnO4: 2MnO4− + 5H2O2 + 6H+ → 2Mn2+ + 5O2 + 8H2O.
  • Reducing (basic): 2MnO4− + 3H2O2 → 2MnO2 + 3O2 + 2OH− + 2H2O.

Storage and uses

H2O2 decomposes (2H2O2 → 2H2O + O2) in light, dust, alkali or metal ions, so it is stored in dark, wax-lined bottles, kept cool, with a trace of stabiliser (urea or phosphoric acid). It is used as an antiseptic, a mild bleach, in restoring paintings, rocket propellant and pollution control.

Dihydrogen as a fuel

Hydrogen is an excellent fuel: its combustion (2H2 + O2 → 2H2O) releases a very high energy per gram (about 143 kJ g−1, far more than petrol) and the only product is water, so it is non-polluting. The vision of a hydrogen economy is to transport and store energy as hydrogen rather than as electricity or fossil fuels. In a fuel cell hydrogen and oxygen react electrochemically to generate electricity directly and efficiently, with water as the only by-product — the technology that powered the Apollo spacecraft. The main challenges are the safe, compact storage of a light, flammable gas and producing hydrogen cheaply without releasing CO2.

examples.problem: Describe the open-book structure of hydrogen peroxide and state the gas-phase dihedral angle.
examples.solution:
1. H2O2 is non-planar: the two O–H bonds lie in two different planes that meet along the central O–O bond.
  2. The shape resembles a half-open book, hence the name open-book structure.
  3. In the gas phase the angle between the two planes (the dihedral angle) is about 111°.

Answer: A non-planar open-book structure with a gas-phase dihedral angle of about 111°.

examples.problem: Write the laboratory preparation of hydrogen peroxide from barium peroxide.
examples.solution:
1. Add cold dilute sulphuric acid to hydrated barium peroxide.
  2. The reaction is BaO2·8H2O + H2SO4 → BaSO4 + H2O2 + 8H2O.
  3. The insoluble BaSO4 is filtered off, leaving a solution of H2O2.

Answer: BaO2·8H2O + H2SO4 → BaSO4↓ + H2O2 + 8H2O.

examples.problem: Why can hydrogen peroxide act both as an oxidising agent and as a reducing agent?
examples.solution:
1. In H2O2 the oxidation state of oxygen is −1.
  2. This is intermediate between 0 (in O2) and −2 (in H2O).
  3. So oxygen can either be reduced to −2 (acting as oxidiser) or oxidised to 0 (acting as reducer), depending on the other reactant.

Answer: Because oxygen is in the intermediate −1 state, H2O2 can both gain and lose electrons.

examples.problem: Write the equation showing hydrogen peroxide acting as a reducing agent towards acidified potassium permanganate.
examples.solution:
1. Acidified KMnO4 (Mn in +7) is reduced to Mn2+.
  2. H2O2 is oxidised, releasing O2.
  3. Balanced: 2MnO4− + 5H2O2 + 6H+ → 2Mn2+ + 5O2 + 8H2O.

Answer: 2MnO4− + 5H2O2 + 6H+ → 2Mn2+ + 5O2 + 8H2O; the pink colour is discharged.

examples.problem: Why is hydrogen peroxide stored in dark, wax-lined bottles, and what stabiliser is added?
examples.solution:
1. H2O2 decomposes to water and oxygen: 2H2O2 → 2H2O + O2.
  2. Decomposition is speeded up by light, heat, dust, alkali and metal ions, so it is kept cool in dark plastic or wax-lined bottles away from rough glass surfaces.
  3. A trace of stabiliser such as urea or phosphoric acid is added to slow the decomposition.

Answer: To prevent light/surface-catalysed decomposition; a trace of urea or phosphoric acid is added as stabiliser.

examples.problem: State two advantages and one challenge of using dihydrogen as a fuel.
examples.solution:
1. Advantage 1: it has a very high energy output per gram (about 143 kJ g−1), much higher than petrol.
  2. Advantage 2: its combustion (2H2 + O2 → 2H2O) gives only water, so it is non-polluting.
  3. Challenge: it is a light, highly flammable gas that is difficult and expensive to store and transport safely, and producing it cleanly is costly.

Answer: Advantages: very high energy per gram and clean (only water); challenge: safe, compact storage and cheap clean production.

recap: H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> is prepared in the lab from BaO<sub>2</sub>·8H<sub>2</sub>O + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> and industrially by the anthraquinone (2-ethylanthraquinol) process.
It has a non-planar open-book structure with a gas-phase dihedral angle of about 111° and an O–O bond of about 148 pm.
Because oxygen is in the −1 state, H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> acts both as an oxidising agent (e.g. PbS → PbSO<sub>4</sub>) and as a reducing agent (e.g. decolourising acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub>).
It is stored in dark, wax-lined bottles, kept cool, with urea or phosphoric acid as stabiliser, because it decomposes to water and oxygen.
Dihydrogen is a clean, high-energy fuel (only water on combustion) central to the hydrogen economy and fuel cells; safe storage and cheap clean production are the main hurdles.

quiz.q: The structure of hydrogen peroxide is best described as:
quiz.explanation: H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> is non-planar, with the two O–H bonds in different planes meeting along the O–O bond, like a half-open book.

quiz.q: The oxidation state of oxygen in hydrogen peroxide is:
quiz.explanation: Oxygen is in the −1 state, intermediate between 0 and −2, which lets H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> act as both oxidiser and reducer.

quiz.q: When H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> decolourises acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub>, it behaves as:
quiz.explanation: It reduces Mn in +7 to Mn<sup>2+</sup> while being oxidised to O<sub>2</sub>, so here H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> is the reducing agent.

quiz.q: A major advantage of dihydrogen as a fuel is that its combustion produces:
quiz.explanation: 2H<sub>2</sub> + O<sub>2</sub> → 2H<sub>2</sub>O gives only water, making hydrogen a clean, non-polluting fuel.

questions.q: The electronic configuration of a hydrogen atom is:
questions.explanation: Hydrogen has one electron in the 1s orbital: 1s<sup>1</sup>.

questions.q: Hydrogen resembles halogens because it can:
options: form a diatomic molecule and gain an electron to give H<sup>−</sup>
questions.explanation: Like halogens it is diatomic (H<sub>2</sub>) and is one electron short of a noble gas, forming H<sup>−</sup>.

questions.q: The number of neutrons in tritium is:
questions.explanation: Tritium (<sup>3</sup>H) has mass number 3 and one proton, so it has 2 neutrons.

questions.q: Water gas is a mixture of:
questions.explanation: C + H<sub>2</sub>O → CO + H<sub>2</sub>; the mixture of CO and H<sub>2</sub> is water gas.

questions.q: In the laboratory dihydrogen is prepared by reacting zinc with:
questions.explanation: Zn + dilute H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → ZnSO<sub>4</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>.

questions.q: Which of the following is a covalent (molecular) hydride?
questions.explanation: NH<sub>3</sub> is formed by a p-block non-metal as discrete molecules, a covalent hydride.

questions.q: On electrolysis of a molten ionic hydride, hydrogen is liberated at the anode because hydrogen is present as:
questions.explanation: Ionic hydrides contain H<sup>−</sup>, which migrates to the anode and is oxidised to H<sub>2</sub>.

questions.q: The H–O–H bond angle in a water molecule is about:
questions.explanation: Lone-pair repulsion compresses the angle in the bent water molecule to about 104.5°.

questions.q: Temporary hardness of water is due to:
questions.explanation: Temporary hardness is caused by soluble bicarbonates of calcium and magnesium.

questions.q: Clark's method removes temporary hardness by adding:
questions.explanation: Ca(HCO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> + Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> → 2CaCO<sub>3</sub>↓ + 2H<sub>2</sub>O.

questions.q: Permanent hardness of water can be removed by:
questions.explanation: Permanent hardness (chlorides/sulphates) needs ion exchange; boiling does not work.

questions.q: When exhausted, sodium zeolite is regenerated by treating it with:
questions.explanation: CaZ + 2NaCl → Na<sub>2</sub>Z + CaCl<sub>2</sub>; brine restores the sodium form.

questions.q: Heavy water is chiefly used as a:
questions.explanation: D<sub>2</sub>O slows fast neutrons without absorbing them, acting as a moderator.

questions.q: The oxidation state of oxygen in hydrogen peroxide is:
questions.explanation: Each oxygen in H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> is in the −1 state, intermediate between 0 and −2.

questions.q: The structure of hydrogen peroxide is:
questions.explanation: H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> is non-planar with a dihedral (open-book) shape.

questions.q: When acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub> is decolourised by H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, the peroxide acts as a(n):
questions.explanation: It reduces Mn(+7) to Mn<sup>2+</sup> while being oxidised to O<sub>2</sub>, so it is a reducing agent.

questions.q: Hydrogen peroxide turns black PbS to white PbSO<sub>4</sub>. Here it acts as a(n):
questions.explanation: It oxidises sulphide to sulphate, so it acts as an oxidising agent (used in restoring paintings).

questions.q: The major product of the complete combustion of dihydrogen used as a fuel is:
questions.explanation: 2H<sub>2</sub> + O<sub>2</sub> → 2H<sub>2</sub>O; only water is formed, making it a clean fuel.

questions.q: Which statement about the isotopes of hydrogen is INCORRECT?
options: They have the same number of protons
They have different numbers of neutrons
They have different chemical formulae for their oxides
questions.explanation: All isotopes form the same kinds of compounds; only physical properties and reaction rates differ, not the chemical formulae.

questions.q: In which medium is the reaction 2MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> + 3H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> → 2MnO<sub>2</sub> + 3O<sub>2</sub> + 2OH<sup>−</sup> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O carried out, and what is H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>'s role?
questions.explanation: The OH<sup>−</sup> product shows a basic medium; H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> reduces Mn(+7) to MnO<sub>2</sub>, so it is the reducing agent.

questions.q: 20 volume hydrogen peroxide means 1 mL of the solution liberates at STP:
questions.explanation: Volume strength is the volume of O<sub>2</sub> at STP given by 1 volume of the solution on decomposition; so 1 mL gives 20 mL O<sub>2</sub>.

questions.q: Which set is correctly matched (hydride : type)?
questions.explanation: B<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub> is a covalent (electron-deficient) hydride; CaH<sub>2</sub>/NaH are ionic and PdH<sub>0.6</sub> is metallic.

questions.q: The water-gas shift reaction CO + H<sub>2</sub>O → CO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub> is used to:
options: increase the yield of H<sub>2</sub> and remove CO
questions.explanation: It converts CO to CO<sub>2</sub> (later scrubbed out) while generating extra H<sub>2</sub>, raising purity and yield.

questions.q: The relatively high boiling point of water compared with H<sub>2</sub>S is mainly due to:
questions.explanation: Oxygen's high electronegativity gives strong O–H···O hydrogen bonds, raising water's boiling point above H<sub>2</sub>S.

questions.q: Demineralised water from a two-bed ion-exchange plant is obtained because:
options: cations are replaced by H<sup>+</sup> and anions by OH<sup>−</sup>, which combine to water
questions.explanation: The cation resin gives H<sup>+</sup> and the anion resin gives OH<sup>−</sup>; these combine to water, removing all ions.

questions.q: Why does deuterium undergo reactions more slowly than protium?
options: the heavier D forms stronger bonds (kinetic isotope effect)
questions.explanation: The greater mass of D strengthens its bonds and raises activation energy, slowing reaction rates.

questions.q: The approximate dihedral angle of H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> changes from the gas to the solid phase as:
questions.explanation: In the gas phase the dihedral angle is about 111°; in the solid it decreases to about 90° due to hydrogen bonding.

questions.q: The 'hydride gap' refers to the fact that:
options: elements of groups 7 to 9 of the d-block generally do not form hydrides
questions.explanation: The transition metals of groups 7–9 generally fail to form stable hydrides, a region called the hydride gap.

questions.q: Which best explains why a hydrogen fuel cell is more efficient than burning hydrogen in an engine?
options: chemical energy is converted directly to electricity without a heat-engine step
it stores hydrogen as a solid
questions.explanation: A fuel cell avoids the thermodynamic (Carnot) losses of a heat engine by converting chemical energy straight to electrical energy.

questions.q: When 1 mol of CaH<sub>2</sub> reacts completely with water, the number of moles of H<sub>2</sub> produced is:
questions.explanation: CaH<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O → Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>; the H<sup>−</sup> and H<sup>+</sup> combine, giving 2 mol H<sub>2</sub>.
